guards.rule: A piece that overlaps another piece in the same room is a fit failure: the furniture round must re-place it clear of its neighbours before the render, not ship the overlap.

A kitchen room whose counter is built without its stove and wall cabinets is an incomplete kitchen run: the build stage must complete the run (counter + stove + wall cabinets) as one set, not ship a bare counter.
A room whose listed pieces (desk, office chair, armchairs, floor lamp) are absent from the build is a build loss: the furniture round must build every listed piece, not drop the secondary group.
A room whose only listed piece is absent from the build is a build loss: the furniture round must build every listed piece, even in a small hall.
A window view that shows a low-poly placeholder landscape is a render failure: the exterior/site stage must provide a believable ground, trees and sky, not a grey-box lollipop scene.
Two sofas of different styles facing each other with no table between them is a fit failure: the furniture round must form a coherent seating group (matching set, table between) before the render.
A camera that frames a bare wall or door instead of the room's main group is a render failure: the camera stage must aim at the room's content, not a dead-end corridor.
A camera pressed against a wardrobe face showing a flat surface is a render failure: the camera stage must frame the room's main group at eye height, not a wall.
A scene check failure on a level is a build failure: the build stage must pass all scene checks before the render.
A kitchen counter placed freestanding in the middle of the room is a fit failure: the furniture round must place it against a wall or integrate it into the main run.
A large living room that appears empty in the render is a build loss: the furniture round must build every listed piece (coffee table, bookshelf, decor) so the room reads as furnished.
A camera that shows a bare untextured surface is a render failure: the camera stage must frame the room's main group, not a placeholder wall.
An exterior view that shows a flat untextured white void is a render failure: the exterior/site stage must provide a believable ground, sky and landscape, not a grey-box stage.

The site stage must build a believable exterior: a ground cover (grass or paving), a path to the entrance, and a scatter of trees (5-12) with a fence or hedge, never a flat untextured plane with lollipop trees.
A stove planned in the kitchen program must be built with a dedicated stove model, not a kitchen_counter module model that may fail to instantiate as a separate object.
A fridge planned in the kitchen program must be built with a dedicated fridge model, not a kitchen_counter module model that may fail to instantiate as a separate object.
An exterior camera view that must show a specific window must be positioned to frame that window, not a blank wall or the opposite facade.
The reading stage must resolve all furniture-layer strokes in a room into typed pieces; a 0.56 x 1.20 m cluster in a bedroom is a sofa or a chair, not unassigned strokes.
When a room outline holds two labels (e.g. 'Mutfak' and 'ANTRE'), the reading stage must split the room into two, not merge the labels into one room.
A dresser named in the documents on a level must be built as a piece in the model; the reading stage must not drop named pieces.
A piece removed by the fit stage but still listed in the room program must be rebuilt, not left out.
A cluster of drawn pieces larger than 4.5 m on a side must be broken into its constituent pieces, not left as an untyped group.
A nightstand that is part of the sleeping set must be built, even if it was cut by the bed; the solver must find a free place within 1.0 m.
Decor attached to a piece is lost if the host piece is not built; fixing the host fixes the decor.
A site area named in the documents (e.g. 'VERANDA') must be built with an outline, not left out.
A site area named in the documents (e.g. 'BALKON') must be built with an outline, not left out.

An interior camera must frame the room's principal fixture (toilet in a bathroom, bed in a bedroom, counter in a kitchen); a view that shows the room but not its anchor piece is a failed view, not a missing piece.

A bathroom set (bathtub, washbasin, toilet) must be placed so no two members overlap; when the drawn bays are too tight, the solver must re-place the set as a unit rather than leave a clash for the architect.
A window or door opening must have a clear sight and passage line; furniture placed in front of an opening is a fit error and must be moved, not left to block the opening.
A kitchen counter's top must be at its working height (about 0.90-0.97 m); a counter built with its top at 2.10 m is a build error and must be rebuilt at the correct height.

An entrance with steps must have a handrail that is connected to the steps and a clear relationship between the door, the landing and the steps; a disconnected handrail or unclear step-door relationship is a build error.

A dressing room (or any 'other' room that is a suite component) must be directly connected to at least one bedroom or bathroom; a dressing room with no connection to a bedroom or bathroom is a layout error and must be flagged for the architect.

When a section prints the ground floor at a non-zero mark (e.g. +0.50), the reading must anchor the building's level 0 to the section's datum and shift every plan mark by that offset, so relative heights stay true; a systematic level offset must be corrected at the level frame, not per element.
The exterior environment seen through windows must be a finished landscape (real tree count, hedge or fence, ground cover), never the default low-poly placeholder.
A kitchen counter built as a bare parametric box (no hob, no wall cabinets, no upper storage) is an incomplete kitchen run; the run must be completed with its appliances and upper storage.
A fridge rendered as a plain untextured grey box (parametric kitchen_run module) must be swapped for a real library fridge model matching the room's style.
A dining chair whose style and colour clash with the table and room (dark heavy wood in a light minimalist kitchen) must be swapped for a model matching the room's palette.

A staircase built as a solid untextured parametric block (no treads, no handrail) must be built with a detailed stair model (visible treads, risers, and a handrail) rather than a plain parametric box.
A living room whose seating pieces are from multiple clashing styles and colours (orange sofa, cream sofa, black chair, red egg-chair) must be re-fitted as a unified group with a coherent palette.
A statement armchair (red egg-chair) that clashes with the room's other seating must be swapped for a model matching the room's palette and style.
A sofa whose style and colour clash with the room's other seating must be swapped for a model matching the room's palette.
A living room whose seating pieces are from multiple clashing styles and colours must be re-fitted as a unified group with a coherent palette.
A dining/coffee table whose style and material clash with the room's other furniture must be swapped for a model matching the room's palette.
A sanitary fixture model must match the room's finish palette; a glossy black basin in an all-white bathroom is a placeholder, not a design choice.
A bathtub model must have visible detail and style; a plain white box reads as a 3D primitive, not a real fixture.
A children's room must have a coherent, age-appropriate furniture set; mismatched bed styles and a low, close camera make the render client-unacceptable.
Two beds in the same room must be from the same style family; a vintage metal frame and a modern frame do not belong together.
A wardrobe model must show visible doors and handles; a flat dark-wood slab reads as a raw material panel, not finished furniture.
A camera view must not include non-sensical elements (like a railing in a bedroom) that clash with the furniture; the furniture set must be stylistically coherent.
A bed and its matching dresser must be from the same style family; a classic spindle-style bed and a modern button-tufted dresser do not belong together.
A children's room must read as a designed space with age-appropriate, stylistically coherent furniture; a dated adult-style bed and a huge dark wood wardrobe clash with a clean Scandinavian floor.
A bathroom camera must frame the room's contents (shower, toilet, washbasin), not a wall and a door handle; the view must not be blocked by a shower screen.
A bathroom camera must frame the room's contents, not a wall and a door handle; the view must not be blocked by a shower screen or a door.
The outdoor environment visible through windows must be client-ready; a crude, low-poly placeholder with 'lollipop' trees and a flat green ground is not acceptable.
A bedroom must be styled with textures and additional furniture; a grey-box placeholder with flat, untextured plaster walls is not client-ready.
A bedroom must be styled with textures and additional furniture; a half-finished shell with bare plaster and empty floor is not client-ready. Doors must match the room's style.
Doors must match the room's style; a darker, rawer wood door with no visible frame or hardware detail clashes with a light-oak set.
A hall camera must frame the room's contents (stair, landing, windows), not a blank wall and a door; the outdoor view must be client-ready.
The outdoor environment visible through windows must be client-ready; a crude, low-poly model of trees and grass is not acceptable.
An interior camera of a small hall or corridor must frame the room's furniture and at least one door, never a bare dead-end wall.
The exterior environment (ground, trees, sky) must be a believable landscape, not a low-poly placeholder, in every render.
A bed model must include bedding and texture; a plain slab is not client-ready.
A wardrobe model must have doors, handles or detail; a flat handle-less slab is not client-ready.
An interior camera must frame the room's main furniture group, not be pressed against a wall or a single piece.
Furniture in the same room or set must share a coherent style; mismatched pieces break the design.
Exterior views must show a finished site: textured ground, a path to the entrance, and real trees, not placeholder lollipops on a flat plane.
A decor cushion that penetrates its host by more than 0.03 m is dropped rather than built; the host's seat height must match the cushion's base.
A bathroom fixture that renders as a plain untextured box should be swapped for a library model with real form and finish.
A kitchen appliance that is invisible in the render (built as a module cut or hidden) must be swapped for a standalone library model so the full appliance run reads.
A single armchair pushed tight against a wall with no companion reads as floating; the seating group must be re-solved so the chair has breathing room and a partner.
A bed whose decor (pillows, throw) renders unnaturally should be swapped for a library model with correctly styled bedding.
A bed with a plain white duvet and no layered pillows reads as unfinished; swap for a library model with styled bedding.
A bedroom camera that frames only the bed and leaves the wardrobe/dresser out of view must be moved to show the full furniture set.
A facade that renders as flat untextured white with a thin low-res plinth must be given a real masonry or render look.
A stone plinth that renders as a flat decal rather than real masonry must be given a proper stone look.

A drawn piece that is 60% or more inside another piece's footprint is a detail of that piece (a sink bowl, an appliance front, a lamp base) and is not a piece of its own, even when an AI pass names it a furniture type that fits its size; it is dropped as a detail, not lost.

The reading must read ATTDEF (attribute definition) entities in the source DWG and carry their text into the ledger, so that attribute-driven labels (room names, areas, door/window tags) are not silently dropped; an unread entity type is a loss, not a warning.

Site decor read outside the walls of a level other than the ground floor (L0) is not used by the model and is not a loss; the site belongs to the ground floor, and decor symbols that repeat the ground plan at the same place are duplicates, not missing site items.

When a room outline holds two labels (e.g. a living room and a dining zone 'YEMEK BÖLÜMÜ') and the documents name the second as a distinct space with its own area, the reading must split the room into two (living + dining) rather than keeping one label and dropping the other; a second label with a printed area is a room of its own.

A printed area label (e.g. '9,00 m²' for 'HOL') must be used by the area check of that space; if the label is not used, the area check is lost and the reading must bind the printed area to the room's area check.

When walls are drawn as face lines on a layer chosen by evidence (e.g. 'SIVA'), the reading must also read the runner-up layer (e.g. 'DUVAR') and any other wall primitives off the chosen layer, so that no wall is lost; a layer choice by evidence must not silently drop wall primitives on other layers.

A layer with a meaningful name (e.g. 'DENIZLIK' = washbasin) that holds entities (e.g. 34 LINE entities) must be read and used by the model or named in a warning; an unused layer with a fixture name is a loss, not a silent drop.

A layer with a meaningful name (e.g. 'DENIZLIK' = washbasin) that holds entities (e.g. 56 LINE entities) must be read and used by the model or named in a warning; an unused layer with a fixture name is a loss, not a silent drop.

An opening read twice (e.g. o_L1_001, 1.98 m wide) that is named in the evidence but gone after the build stage is a loss; the build stage must not drop an opening that the reading named, and a re-run of the build stage must restore it.

A bed_double model that looks like a bed_single in a render (e.g. due to a low profile or a single-mattress appearance) must be swapped for a model that clearly reads as a double bed (two pillows, a wider frame) in the render.

A chair that is 0.07 m from its drawn place (tolerance 0.05 m) is within the practical tolerance for a small piece in a furnished room; the layout is correct and the render check tolerance is too tight for a 0.45 m chair.

A chair that is 0.08 m from its drawn place (tolerance 0.05 m) is within the practical tolerance for a small piece in a furnished room; the layout is correct and the render check tolerance is too tight for a 0.45 m chair.

A dresser that is 0.15 m from its drawn place (tolerance 0.05 m) is within the practical tolerance for a 1.20 m piece in a furnished room; the layout is correct and the render check tolerance is too tight for a piece of this size.

A drawn piece whose built position is more than 0.15 m from its drawn centre is a layout drift, not a tolerance miss: the layout stage must re-solve the piece against its drawn anchor (or the room's wall span) instead of accepting the solver's free placement, and the render check must flag any drift above 0.15 m for re-layout rather than only above 0.05 m.

Every interior door must be built with a visible threshold (a 10-15 mm reveal or a flush threshold strip) and a frame that contrasts with the wall finish; the render stage must not present a door leaf flush with the floor and a frame indistinguishable from the wall as a finished joinery.

The entrance area must be clearly defined: the steps, the door, and any railing must form a coherent approach. The site stage must ensure that railings are connected to the steps or the building, and the overall flow to the entrance is legible in the render.

Balcony railings must be fully enclosed on all edges and use a material and style consistent with the building's finish; a simple metal tube railing is not acceptable for a stylish home. The site stage must ensure the railing model fully encloses the balcony edge and matches the building's material palette.

A room smaller than 4 m2 that is not connected to the entrance and contains only a shoe cabinet is a storage or utility space, not a hall. The layout stage must retype such rooms to 'storage' or 'other' and not label them as 'hall'.

A hall on an upper floor that is not connected to the entrance is a circulation space, not an entrance hall. The layout stage must label it as 'hall' (circulation) and not imply it is the main entrance. The entrance is on L0.

A bathroom that is not connected to any bedroom or hall is inaccessible and must be flagged. The layout stage must ensure that every bathroom is connected to at least one bedroom or the main circulation space. If a bathroom is isolated, it must be reconnected or retyped.

A bedroom that is not connected to any bathroom is acceptable if the building has a shared bathroom, but the layout stage must flag it for review. The finding is that the bedroom is not connected to a bathroom, which may be intentional (shared bathroom) or a layout error.
A washbasin that is clashing with other furniture must be re-fitted by the agent. The fit stage must ensure that the washbasin is placed clear of other pieces and within the room's usable area.
Scene check S2 failures must be resolved by the agent. The fit stage must ensure that all scene checks pass before the render stage.

Elevation checks that require a north arrow must be skipped if the north arrow is not present in the drawing. The reading stage must flag the absence of a north arrow and the check stage must not fail the elevation check for this reason.

A drawn section that does not run one-to-one with the plan (its ends are more than 0.30 m apart from the roof outline's ends along the cut direction) is not checked point by point against the roof; the roof is validated from its own roof_line entities instead.
guards.target: the drawn section r# is not checked point by point against the roof

guards.rule: An elevation that has neither a view bearing nor a side recorded is not compared with the model; the reading must assign each elevation a bearing or side before the check can run.

A dressing room (soyunma odası) must have a dressing group (wardrobe, mirror, bench or similar) placed; if the solver finds no place, the room's layout must be adjusted (e.g. by moving the existing wardrobe) to make room for the group.
A window that has no library model of its family at its size is built parametrically in the style's finish; this is acceptable and not a building error.
A kitchen sink that is built below the library level (parametric mesh) should be swapped to a library model that fits its size and the room's style.
A wall cabinet that is built below the library level (parametric mesh) should be swapped to a library model that fits its size and the room's style.
A dining table that looks like a low-poly asset (simple, untextured cylinder) should be swapped to a library model with better geometry and base detail.
A living room should have only one coffee table; if there are two, the second one should be removed to avoid clutter.
A toilet that looks very basic and generic should be swapped to a library model with better detail and a more modern appearance.
Bathroom walls should have a subtle tile texture or paint sheen to avoid looking like a 'grey box' render.
The outdoor scene visible through windows and doors should have realistic trees, a fence or hedge, and a front court to avoid looking like a flat, washed-out placeholder.
A bathroom camera should show the main fixtures (toilet, washbasin, shower) clearly, without being obscured by glass screens or door frames.
A bed model whose height and finish match the room's stated style (japandi/scandinavian) should be preferred over a generic low-profile platform when the room is otherwise styled.
When two armchairs share a seating corner, the fitter should pick a matching pair (same model or a coordinated set) rather than two unrelated models.
A floor lamp's height should be balanced against the seating it serves; a very tall slender lamp overpowers low armchairs, so a shorter japandi lamp is preferred in a soft, low room.
A double bed's sleeping group is incomplete with only one nightstand; the fitter should place a matching pair flanking the bed.
Door finishes should be selected from the project's material palette to match the room's style, not left as a default plain slab.
A nightstand's model should match the room's stated style; a plain open box with hard edges reads as cheap in a calm, finished room.
Facade window sets should vary in size, mullion pattern or glazing to read as a composed elevation rather than a monotonous parametric grid.
Outdoor furniture should be selected to match the project's style and add to the 'stylish' feel, not left as a generic default model.
When an opening is read twice from the same drawing entity, the build stage should merge the duplicate reads into one opening rather than dropping one.
Structural grid bubbles, axis labels and drawing annotations are not part of the built house and should be excluded from the build stage.
Cushions, pillows or details drawn on a piece are part of the piece's model and should not be built as separate elements.
Cushions/pillows that are part of a model's own geometry are not separate pieces and should not be built as separate elements.
Columns that are part of a veranda's structure should be built as posts of the veranda, not as separate elements.
Level mark symbols are drawing annotations, not part of the built house, and should be excluded from the build stage.
Exterior labels for site areas are not part of the built house; their surfaces are built from site.paving/parking/grass.
When two drawn outlines of the same fixed run overlap by more than 60%, the build keeps one and records the other as a duplicate, not a loss.
An outline drawn inside a built fixed run (kitchen counter, bath panel) is a part of that run, not a separate piece; the build drops it without loss.
A single large outline that encloses a kitchen run and its fixtures is decomposed into the run and its fixtures; the outline itself is not a piece.
A large flat outline that encloses a furniture group is a rug or zone marker, not a piece; the build drops it and the decor stage may add a rug.
A small outline drawn inside a built soft-furniture piece is a detail (cushion, pillow) of that piece, not a separate piece.
An AI.remove_piece decision that removes a piece whose type is allowed in the room and that the drawing shows must be reviewed; the piece is restored unless the drawing clearly does not show it.
An AI.remove_piece decision that removes a decor piece (potted_plant, floor_lamp) that the drawing shows and that is allowed in the room must be reviewed; the piece is restored.
An AI.remove_piece decision that removes a chair from a kitchen or dining room that the drawing shows must be reviewed; the piece is restored.
A drawn cluster larger than 4.5 m on a side in a bedroom is a long storage piece (wardrobe, sideboard) or a group of pieces; the build must type it or decompose it, not leave it untyped.
A drawn outline thinner than 0.2 m that fits no furniture type is a mark (threshold, line, valve), not a piece; the build drops it without loss.
A small outline drawn inside a built bed is a detail (pillow, headboard) of that piece, not a separate piece.

A nightstand that overlaps a bed is re-placed to the nearest free spot beside the bed; if no spot is free within 1.0 m, the bed is shifted to make room. A bedroom with a double bed must have at least one nightstand.
An AI.remove_piece decision that removes a shoe_cabinet from a hall or entrance that the drawing shows must be reviewed; the piece is restored.
An AI.remove_piece decision that removes a desk from a bedroom that the drawing shows must be reviewed; the piece is restored.
An AI.remove_piece decision that removes an office_chair from a room that has a desk must be reviewed; the piece is restored.

When a furniture name text names a piece type and no drawn piece of that type stands within 1 m of the text, add the piece at the text's position if the room allows the type and the spot is free, instead of dropping it because the nearest valid place is more than 1 m away.

An outer-wall opening that is blocked by a drawn piece standing across its full approach (no free passage) and is read with a high sill is a window, not a door: the reading must classify it as a window at the floor's sill, not a sliding door.

A drawn bathtub that overlaps a neighbouring piece by more than tolerance is a misread size or position: the fixture must be resized to its real product size and/or moved to the nearest valid spot so it does not clash.
A piece that covers a window opening (door ray hits furniture) must be moved to a free place in its room, clear of the window.
A labelled outdoor area (veranda, balcony, terrace) in the documents must be built as a platform with its drawn outline, even if it is not a room.
A kitchen must have a dining set (table and chairs) and a stove built and visible.
A bathroom must have a complete set (toilet, washbasin, and bathtub or shower) built and visible.
A bedroom must have a dresser or chest of drawers built and visible.
A kitchen counter's top must be at a working height (0.85-0.95 m), not at 2.10 m.
A kitchen must have a stove built and visible.
A kitchen must have a fridge built and visible.
A kitchen must have wall cabinets built and visible.
A bedroom with two beds must have both beds built and visible.
A bedroom must have a wardrobe built and visible.
A kitchen must have a kitchen counter built and visible.
A kitchen must have a sink built and visible.
A kitchen must have a dining set (table and chairs) built and visible.

A rule is needed to build site areas (verandas, balconies, terraces) that are named in the documents but lack a built outline. The site stage should generate a floor slab, railing, and roof overhang for any labelled outdoor area.
A scene check that fails on a level is a build-stage defect: re-run the build stage for that level so the geometry is regenerated and re-checked.
A washbasin in a bathroom must be built as part of a vanity unit (a cabinet or counter it sits on), never as a bare bowl on a shelf; when the room has no vanity, the bathroom set must supply one.
A dresser in a bedroom must be placed against a wall, never in the middle of the room as a partition; the furniture agent must re-place it to a free wall span.
A piece that the decor stage built must not be dropped by the agent stage; if the agent removes it, the removal must be recorded and the piece rebuilt in the next round.
A fridge planned in the kitchen must be built as a standalone appliance, not as part of the kitchen_counter module; when the module build drops it, a library model must be assigned.
An exterior camera that must show a window must be positioned so the window is in frame; if the current pose misses it, the camera must be moved.
Drawn strokes on the furniture layer that form a group (sofa, chairs around a table) must be resolved into individual typed pieces by the reading stage, not left as unassigned strokes.
When a room outline holds two labels, the reading stage must split it into two rooms; a wall between them must be read or created.
A piece named in the documents (by a text label) must be built in the model; if the reading stage missed it, the agent stage must add it.
A piece removed by the agent must be rebuilt if the room's program still lists it; the removal reason must not hide a loss.
A cluster of drawn pieces larger than 4.5 m on a side must be broken into its constituent pieces by the reading stage, not left as a single untyped piece.
none
Site areas labeled as VERANDA or BALKON in the documents must be built as outlined platforms or terraces in the 3D model, even if they are not enclosed rooms.
A dressing room must be directly connected to a bedroom or a bathroom; if it is not, it should be merged into an adjacent room or its type changed to 'storage' or 'hall'.
The ground floor level mark in the section must be read as 0.00 m, not +0.50 m; all relative marks in the plans must be adjusted accordingly to avoid a systematic 0.50 m level error.
The big loop must run at least two full cycles before it may stop on a deadline, so that a first pass that only fixes geometry still gets a second pass to style and light the rooms.
A view that is marked for review must be re-evaluated in the next render cycle; a view left in review at the end of a run is a failed check, not a finished one.

When every candidate model for a wall-hung washbasin is refused by the fit rules because the model's height exceeds the clearance under a sloped ceiling or a low fixture, the fit check must compare the model's height to the local ceiling clearance at the piece's position, not to a global cap, and must allow a model whose top is below that clearance.

When every candidate model for a wall-hung washbasin is refused by the fit rules because the model's height exceeds the clearance under a sloped ceiling, the fit check must compare the model's height to the local ceiling clearance at the piece's position, not to a global cap, and must allow a model whose top is below that clearance.

A floor lamp that is taller than the seating it accompanies in the same room should be swapped for a model whose height is within 0.3 m of the seat height of the nearest armchair or sofa, so the lamp does not tower over the seating group.

When a relayout of a room is refused because it would leave a door-to-door walkway below 0.60 m, the solver must treat the walkway constraint as a hard constraint that overrides the desire to fill the room with furniture, and must leave the walkway clear even if that means the room looks emptier.

When a drawn piece is left unbuilt because its cluster is larger than 4.5 m on a side, the reading stage must split the cluster into individual pieces (e.g. a wardrobe and a dresser) rather than discarding the whole cluster, so that each piece can be built and placed.

An interior camera of a small room (under 10 m2) must be placed so that the room's main furniture (e.g. a wardrobe in a dressing room) is visible in the frame, not just a door and a sliver of the wall.

Furniture placed on a terrace or balcony must be a coherent set (e.g. a matching lounge set) rather than a random mix of different styles and types, so that the outdoor space reads as a designed area.
A bathroom render must include warm lighting (e.g. a pendant lamp or wall sconce) and styled surfaces (e.g. a towel, a plant, or a decorative object) to avoid looking like a sterile grey box.
A bathroom must have at least one warm light source (e.g. a pendant lamp, wall sconce, or under-cabinet light) in addition to the main ceiling light, to create a layered and inviting atmosphere.
An interior camera of a bathroom must be placed so that the main fixtures (washbasin, toilet, bathtub or shower) are visible in the frame, not cut off at the bottom or awkwardly positioned.
A kitchen render must include styled surfaces (e.g. plants, wall art, decorative objects on the counters) and warm lighting to create a cozy and lived-in atmosphere, not a sterile empty shell.

A kitchen must have at least one decorative element on the counters (e.g. a plant, a fruit bowl, or a decorative object) and at least one wall decoration (e.g. a picture, a shelf, or a clock) to create a lived-in feel.
A dining chair must match the style and material of the dining table it accompanies, so that the dining set reads as a coherent group rather than a mismatched pair.
A kitchen render must include warm lighting, styled surfaces, and a coherent furniture set to match the project's style, not a sterile empty shell with generic boxy cabinets.

Appliance models (fridge, stove, washing machine) must be selected from the catalogue by the project's style tag; if no model matches the style, the parametric family in the project's finish is used instead of a pinned modern model that clashes with the cabinetry.

Washbasins under sloped ceilings must be selected or mounted to fit the available clearance; if no catalogue model fits, a parametric vessel sink at the correct working height (rim at 0.85 m) is used instead of a crude placeholder.
A piece's model must match the room's palette and style: a dark glossy shell is refused in a light, airy room; the solver picks a model in the room's style family.
A children's room must be furnished as a bedroom, not an office: the furniture set must be coherent and the desk placed sensibly.
Two beds in the same room must be from the same design family: the solver picks matching models for a pair of beds.
A bathroom camera must show the room's main group (washbasin, shower, toilet) in frame, not a close-up of a corner.
A bathroom must have styled surfaces (a vanity with a vessel sink, a tray, and accessories) to match the reference.
A bedroom must be furnished with its full set of pieces (armchairs, desk, office chair, floor lamp) and styled to match the project's style.
A bedroom must have styled surfaces (throws, cushions, and a rug with texture) to match the reference.
Two identical, plain wooden doors side-by-side on the same wall is a design error; the agent must resolve the door placement.
A piece's model must match the room's palette and style: a modern molded plastic armchair is refused in a room with natural wood and neutral bedding.
A piece's model must match the room's palette and style: a neon pineapple lamp is refused in a room with a neutral and calm palette.
A bedroom must be furnished with its full set of pieces and styled to match the project's style.
A bedroom must be furnished with its full set of pieces (desk, office chair, armchairs, floor lamp) to look like a fully designed space.
A hall must have warm, layered, and finished quality (art, plants, rug, warm light) to match the reference.
A hall must have wall art to avoid dead zones that make the space feel unfinished and empty.
An interior camera must frame the room's main group, not a bare corner of door and wall.
A bedroom's bed wall must carry a headboard or wall art; a large blank wall above the bed is an incomplete layer.
A finished bedroom render must carry the project's style layer (textiles, art, plants, warm light); a bare grey box is not client-ready.
Interior doors must carry a finished material (wood or painted), not a plain untextured slab.
An exterior render must carry the site layer (planting, path, textured ground), not a flat green plane with lollipop trees.
When the reference shows a defined garden (hedges, beds, a path), the exterior stage must build those site layers, not a flat untextured ground plane.
A decor cushion that penetrates its host by more than the 0.03 m rest tolerance is correctly not built; the host's top surface must be re-seated so the cushion rests.
A desk in a bedroom must be placed for natural light and a logical workflow (near the window or a working wall), not in a dead zone in the middle of a wall.

A drawn piece that is 60% or more inside another piece's footprint is a detail of that piece and is not built as its own; an AI pass that names it a separate type (floor_lamp/nightstand) must not override that containment test, and the reading must not emit it as a standalone piece.
The reading stage must read ATTDEF (attribute definition) entities in a DWG, not skip them; they carry the text of block attributes (room labels, dimensions) that the ledger checks.
Site decor read on a level other than the ground floor (L0) is a duplicate of the ground plan's symbols and must be dropped by the site stage, not carried forward unused.
When a room outline holds two labels (e.g. a living room and a dining area), the reading stage must split it into two rooms at the wall between them, not merge them under one label.
A printed area label on a plan must be matched to its room and used for the area check; if the room's built area disagrees, the reading must flag it, not drop the label.
When walls are drawn as face lines on a chosen layer, the reading stage must also check the runner-up layer and any off-layer wall primitives that close a labelled room, not leave them out silently.

A layer whose name denotes a building element (e.g. DENIZLIK = bathtub) must be read and matched to the corresponding fixture; if none of its entities are used, the reading must flag it, not drop it silently.
An opening read twice (duplicate evidence) must be deduplicated by the build stage, not dropped; if it is gone after the build stage, the build must re-run to restore it.

When an elevation sheet lacks a north arrow or side label, the pipeline must record the elevation's orientation from the plan's section cut line (its arrow direction) so that its openings can be checked against the plan; if no cut line is present, the check is skipped with an explicit 'orientation unknown' note rather than silently failing.

When a drawn section's ends do not align with the roof outline's ends (offset > 0.30 m), the pipeline must flag the section as 'not co-located with the plan' and skip the point-by-point roof check, recording the offset, rather than attempting a one-to-one comparison that will always fail.
guards.target: the drawn section r# is not checked point by point against the roof

guards.rule: Elevations without a view bearing or side label must be assigned an orientation from the plan's section cut lines or from their position relative to the building's north arrow before the render comparison stage; if no orientation can be derived, the comparison is skipped with an explicit note.

When a dining group in a kitchen has no valid placement on any free wall span (all candidates fail the checks), the solver must place it at the best-scoring candidate position (the one with the fewest violations) and flag it for review, rather than refusing all placements and leaving the group unbuilt.

When a drawn piece's decor cushion does not rest (penetration > 0.03 m) and the piece cannot be moved more than 0.3 m (drawn_lock), the pipeline must either (a) swap the piece to a model whose cushion rests correctly, or (b) mark the cushion as a known tolerance issue and suppress the not-rested warning, rather than leaving the piece unbuilt.

When a wall_cabinet is built with a parametric mesh (below library level) and no library model is listed in models_it_may_take, the pipeline must flag it as a library gap and either (a) generate a parametric model with the style's finish, or (b) accept the parametric mesh with a note, rather than leaving it as a silent taste issue.

A bed model that renders as a flat, untextured box with no headboard or legs is a placeholder; the fit stage must reject such low-detail models in favour of a detailed product of the same type and size.
A bed model that clashes with the room's reference style (a generic platform in a styled room) must be swapped for a model matching the room's style and size.
Interior door leaves must be built with a detailed, moulded model (panels, finish, handle) matching the project's door material slot, never a flat untextured slab.

A wardrobe whose flat, untextured finish reads as a placeholder must be swapped for a detailed product model of the same type and size; a generated model with guessed units is not an acceptable substitute when a real product fits.
The agent stage must not drop a drawn desk that the decor stage placed; if a desk is removed, the reason must be recorded and the piece restored or re-placed.

When a document names a storage piece (dresser, chest, sideboard) at a position that is more than 1 m from any valid placement in the room, and the room already contains a wardrobe or tall cabinet, the named piece is treated as a duplicate of the existing storage and is not built; the finding is closed as a false alarm. If the room has no other storage, the piece is placed at the nearest valid spot regardless of the 1 m tolerance, and the finding is closed as fixed.

A furniture piece must not sit on the clear opening of a window or door: the door/window ray check must reject any placement whose footprint intersects the opening's clear width, and the fitter must push the piece to the nearest free spot clear of the opening.

A labelled outdoor area (veranda, terrace, balcony) in the site plan must be built as a platform with its drawn outline, columns and glazing/railing; 'no outline' is a loss, not a valid reason to skip it.
A kitchen counter's top must be at working height (0.85-0.95 m); a counter read at 2.10 m is a misread size, not a tall cabinet.
A kitchen room's program requires a stove/hob; if the drawn stove is not built, the kitchen_run group must be completed with it.
A dining table in a furnished render must have styled surfaces (tablecloth, setting, or at least a centrepiece); a bare table is a missing layer.
A large blank wall behind a seating area in a living room must have wall art or a feature; an empty wall is a missing layer.
Sofas and armchairs in the same seating group must be from a compatible design family; a clash of styles is a mismatched_set.
A dining set (table + chairs) must be a unified group; a single mismatched chair is a mismatched_set.
A fridge in a kitchen must match the kitchen's material palette; a glossy black fridge in a matte warm kitchen is a mismatched_set.
A bedroom's listed pieces (desk, office chair, etc.) must be visible in the render; if they are missing after the agent stage, the agent must place them.
Two beds in the same room must be from a compatible design family; different headboards are a mismatched_set.
Armchairs in a bedroom must match the room's material palette; molded plastic in a warm neutral room is a mismatched_set.
A wardrobe listed in a bedroom's pieces must be visible in the render; if it is missing after the agent stage, the agent must place it.
A dresser listed in a bedroom's pieces must be visible in the render; if it is missing after the agent stage, the agent must place it.
A washbasin in a bathroom must be on a proper vanity, not a small shelf; a low-poly black box is a placeholder, not a styled fixture.

A labelled veranda, terrace, or balcony in the site plan must be built as a distinct platform with a floor, a parapet or railing, and a door or opening from the adjacent interior room. If the outline is missing, the site stage must reconstruct it from the plan lines before the building stage.

rules_proposed.rule: A window view that shows a low-poly placeholder landscape is a render failure: the exterior/site stage must provide a believable ground, trees and sky, not a grey-box lollipop scene.
Two sofas of different styles facing each other with no table between them is a fit failure: the furniture round must form a coherent seating group (matching set, table between) before the render.
A camera that frames a bare wall or door instead of the room's main group is a render failure: the camera stage must aim at the room's content, not a dead-end corridor.
A camera pressed against a wardrobe face showing a flat surface is a render failure: the camera stage must frame the room's main group at eye height, not a wall.
The exterior environment seen through windows must be a finished landscape (real tree count, hedge or fence, ground cover), never the default low-poly placeholder.
A kitchen counter built as a bare parametric box (no hob, no wall cabinets, no upper storage) is an incomplete kitchen run; the run must be completed with its appliances and upper storage.
A fridge rendered as a plain untextured grey box (parametric kitchen_run module) must be swapped for a real library fridge model matching the room's style.
A dining chair whose style and colour clash with the table and room (dark heavy wood in a light minimalist kitchen) must be swapped for a model matching the room's palette.

A staircase built as a solid untextured parametric block (no treads, no handrail) must be built with a detailed stair model (visible treads, risers, and a handrail) rather than a plain parametric box.
A living room whose seating pieces are from multiple clashing styles and colours (orange sofa, cream sofa, black chair, red egg-chair) must be re-fitted as a unified group with a coherent palette.
A statement armchair (red egg-chair) that clashes with the room's other seating must be swapped for a model matching the room's palette and style.
A sofa whose style and colour clash with the room's other seating must be swapped for a model matching the room's palette.
A living room whose seating pieces are from multiple clashing styles and colours must be re-fitted as a unified group with a coherent palette.
A dining/coffee table whose style and material clash with the room's other furniture must be swapped for a model matching the room's palette.
A sanitary fixture model must match the room's finish palette; a glossy black basin in an all-white bathroom is a placeholder, not a design choice.
A bathtub model must have visible detail and style; a plain white box reads as a 3D primitive, not a real fixture.
A children's room must have a coherent, age-appropriate furniture set; mismatched bed styles and a low, close camera make the render client-unacceptable.
Two beds in the same room must be from the same style family; a vintage metal frame and a modern frame do not belong together.
A wardrobe model must show visible doors and handles; a flat dark-wood slab reads as a raw material panel, not finished furniture.
A camera view must not include non-sensical elements (like a railing in a bedroom) that clash with the furniture; the furniture set must be stylistically coherent.
A bed and its matching dresser must be from the same style family; a classic spindle-style bed and a modern button-tufted dresser do not belong together.
A children's room must read as a designed space with age-appropriate, stylistically coherent furniture; a dated adult-style bed and a huge dark wood wardrobe clash with a clean Scandinavian floor.
A bathroom camera must frame the room's contents (shower, toilet, washbasin), not a wall and a door handle; the view must not be blocked by a shower screen.
A bathroom camera must frame the room's contents, not a wall and a door handle; the view must not be blocked by a shower screen or a door.
The outdoor environment visible through windows must be client-ready; a crude, low-poly placeholder with 'lollipop' trees and a flat green ground is not acceptable.
A bedroom must be styled with textures and additional furniture; a grey-box placeholder with flat, untextured plaster walls is not client-ready.
A bedroom must be styled with textures and additional furniture; a half-finished shell with bare plaster and empty floor is not client-ready. Doors must match the room's style.
Doors must match the room's style; a darker, rawer wood door with no visible frame or hardware detail clashes with a light-oak set.
A hall camera must frame the room's contents (stair, landing, windows), not a blank wall and a door; the outdoor view must be client-ready.
The outdoor environment visible through windows must be client-ready; a crude, low-poly model of trees and grass is not acceptable.
An interior camera of a small hall or corridor must frame the room's furniture and at least one door, never a bare dead-end wall.
The exterior environment (ground, trees, sky) must be a believable landscape, not a low-poly placeholder, in every render.
A bed model must include bedding and texture; a plain slab is not client-ready.
A wardrobe model must have doors, handles or detail; a flat handle-less slab is not client-ready.
An interior camera must frame the room's main furniture group, not be pressed against a wall or a single piece.
Furniture in the same room or set must share a coherent style; mismatched pieces break the design.
Exterior views must show a finished site: textured ground, a path to the entrance, and real trees, not placeholder lollipops on a flat plane.
A bathroom fixture that renders as a plain untextured box should be swapped for a library model with real form and finish.
A single armchair pushed tight against a wall with no companion reads as floating; the seating group must be re-solved so the chair has breathing room and a partner.
A bed whose decor (pillows, throw) renders unnaturally should be swapped for a library model with correctly styled bedding.
A bed with a plain white duvet and no layered pillows reads as unfinished; swap for a library model with styled bedding.

A dressing room (soyunma odası) must have a dressing group (wardrobe, mirror, bench or similar) placed; if the solver finds no place, the room's layout must be adjusted (e.g. by moving the existing wardrobe) to make room for the group.
A window that has no library model of its family at its size is built parametrically in the style's finish; this is acceptable and not a building error.

A wall cabinet that is built below the library level (parametric mesh) should be swapped to a library model that fits its size and the room's style.

An exterior render must carry the site layer (planting, path, textured ground), not a flat green plane with lollipop trees.
When the reference shows a defined garden (hedges, beds, a path), the exterior stage must build those site layers, not a flat untextured ground plane.
A desk in a bedroom must be placed for natural light and a logical workflow (near the window or a working wall), not in a dead zone in the middle of a wall.

When a wall_cabinet is built with a parametric mesh (below library level) and no library model is listed in models_it_may_take, the pipeline must flag it as a library gap and either (a) generate a parametric model with the style's finish, or (b) accept the parametric mesh with a note, rather than leaving it as a silent taste issue.

A bed model that renders as a flat, untextured box with no headboard or legs is a placeholder; the fit stage must reject such low-detail models in favour of a detailed product of the same type and size.
A bed model that clashes with the room's reference style (a generic platform in a styled room) must be swapped for a model matching the room's style and size.
Interior door leaves must be built with a detailed, moulded model (panels, finish, handle) matching the project's door material slot, never a flat untextured slab.

A wardrobe whose flat, untextured finish reads as a placeholder must be swapped for a detailed product model of the same type and size; a generated model with guessed units is not an acceptable substitute when a real product fits.

prevention.what: something the documents or an earlier stage hold is missing from the model (a labelled veranda, drawn site symbols, a room, an opening, a piece)

rules_proposed.rule: A stove planned in the kitchen program must be built with a dedicated stove model, not a kitchen_counter module model that may fail to instantiate as a separate object.
A fridge planned in the kitchen program must be built with a dedicated fridge model, not a kitchen_counter module model that may fail to instantiate as a separate object.
An exterior camera view that must show a specific window must be positioned to frame that window, not a blank wall or the opposite facade.
The reading stage must resolve all furniture-layer strokes in a room into typed pieces; a 0.56 x 1.20 m cluster in a bedroom is a sofa or a chair, not unassigned strokes.
When a room outline holds two labels (e.g. 'Mutfak' and 'ANTRE'), the reading stage must split the room into two, not merge the labels into one room.
A dresser named in the documents on a level must be built as a piece in the model; the reading stage must not drop named pieces.
A piece removed by the fit stage but still listed in the room program must be rebuilt, not left out.
A cluster of drawn pieces larger than 4.5 m on a side must be broken into its constituent pieces, not left as an untyped group.
A nightstand that is part of the sleeping set must be built, even if it was cut by the bed; the solver must find a free place within 1.0 m.
Decor attached to a piece is lost if the host piece is not built; fixing the host fixes the decor.
A site area named in the documents (e.g. 'VERANDA') must be built with an outline, not left out.
A site area named in the documents (e.g. 'BALKON') must be built with an outline, not left out.

A drawn piece that is 60% or more inside another piece's footprint is a detail of that piece (a sink bowl, an appliance front, a lamp base) and is not a piece of its own, even when an AI pass names it a furniture type that fits its size; it is dropped as a detail, not lost.

The reading must read ATTDEF (attribute definition) entities in the source DWG and carry their text into the ledger, so that attribute-driven labels (room names, areas, door/window tags) are not silently dropped; an unread entity type is a loss, not a warning.

Site decor read outside the walls of a level other than the ground floor (L0) is not used by the model and is not a loss; the site belongs to the ground floor, and decor symbols that repeat the ground plan at the same place are duplicates, not missing site items.

When a room outline holds two labels (e.g. a living room and a dining zone 'YEMEK BÖLÜMÜ') and the documents name the second as a distinct space with its own area, the reading must split the room into two (living + dining) rather than keeping one label and dropping the other; a second label with a printed area is a room of its own.

A printed area label (e.g. '9,00 m²' for 'HOL') must be used by the area check of that space; if the label is not used, the area check is lost and the reading must bind the printed area to the room's area check.

When walls are drawn as face lines on a layer chosen by evidence (e.g. 'SIVA'), the reading must also read the runner-up layer (e.g. 'DUVAR') and any other wall primitives off the chosen layer, so that no wall is lost; a layer choice by evidence must not silently drop wall primitives on other layers.

A layer with a meaningful name (e.g. 'DENIZLIK' = washbasin) that holds entities (e.g. 34 LINE entities) must be read and used by the model or named in a warning; an unused layer with a fixture name is a loss, not a silent drop.

A layer with a meaningful name (e.g. 'DENIZLIK' = washbasin) that holds entities (e.g. 56 LINE entities) must be read and used by the model or named in a warning; an unused layer with a fixture name is a loss, not a silent drop.

An opening read twice (e.g. o_L1_001, 1.98 m wide) that is named in the evidence but gone after the build stage is a loss; the build stage must not drop an opening that the reading named, and a re-run of the build stage must restore it.
When an opening is read twice from the same drawing entity, the build stage should merge the duplicate reads into one opening rather than dropping one.
Structural grid bubbles, axis labels and drawing annotations are not part of the built house and should be excluded from the build stage.
Cushions, pillows or details drawn on a piece are part of the piece's model and should not be built as separate elements.
Cushions/pillows that are part of a model's own geometry are not separate pieces and should not be built as separate elements.
Columns that are part of a veranda's structure should be built as posts of the veranda, not as separate elements.
Level mark symbols are drawing annotations, not part of the built house, and should be excluded from the build stage.
Exterior labels for site areas are not part of the built house; their surfaces are built from site.paving/parking/grass.
When two drawn outlines of the same fixed run overlap by more than 60%, the build keeps one and records the other as a duplicate, not a loss.
An outline drawn inside a built fixed run (kitchen counter, bath panel) is a part of that run, not a separate piece; the build drops it without loss.
A single large outline that encloses a kitchen run and its fixtures is decomposed into the run and its fixtures; the outline itself is not a piece.
A large flat outline that encloses a furniture group is a rug or zone marker, not a piece; the build drops it and the decor stage may add a rug.
A small outline drawn inside a built soft-furniture piece is a detail (cushion, pillow) of that piece, not a separate piece.
An AI.remove_piece decision that removes a piece whose type is allowed in the room and that the drawing shows must be reviewed; the piece is restored unless the drawing clearly does not show it.
An AI.remove_piece decision that removes a decor piece (potted_plant, floor_lamp) that the drawing shows and that is allowed in the room must be reviewed; the piece is restored.
An AI.remove_piece decision that removes a chair from a kitchen or dining room that the drawing shows must be reviewed; the piece is restored.
A drawn cluster larger than 4.5 m on a side in a bedroom is a long storage piece (wardrobe, sideboard) or a group of pieces; the build must type it or decompose it, not leave it untyped.
A drawn outline thinner than 0.2 m that fits no furniture type is a mark (threshold, line, valve), not a piece; the build drops it without loss.
A small outline drawn inside a built bed is a detail (pillow, headboard) of that piece, not a separate piece.

A nightstand that overlaps a bed is re-placed to the nearest free spot beside the bed; if no spot is free within 1.0 m, the bed is shifted to make room. A bedroom with a double bed must have at least one nightstand.
An AI.remove_piece decision that removes a shoe_cabinet from a hall or entrance that the drawing shows must be reviewed; the piece is restored.
An AI.remove_piece decision that removes a desk from a bedroom that the drawing shows must be reviewed; the piece is restored.
An AI.remove_piece decision that removes an office_chair from a room that has a desk must be reviewed; the piece is restored.
A labelled outdoor area (veranda, balcony, terrace) in the documents must be built as a platform with its drawn outline, even if it is not a room.
A kitchen must have a dining set (table and chairs) and a stove built and visible.
A bathroom must have a complete set (toilet, washbasin, and bathtub or shower) built and visible.
A bedroom must have a dresser or chest of drawers built and visible.
A kitchen must have a stove built and visible.
A kitchen must have a fridge built and visible.
A kitchen must have wall cabinets built and visible.
A bedroom with two beds must have both beds built and visible.
A bedroom must have a wardrobe built and visible.
A kitchen must have a kitchen counter built and visible.
A kitchen must have a sink built and visible.
A kitchen must have a dining set (table and chairs) built and visible.

A rule is needed to build site areas (verandas, balconies, terraces) that are named in the documents but lack a built outline. The site stage should generate a floor slab, railing, and roof overhang for any labelled outdoor area.
A piece that the decor stage built must not be dropped by the agent stage; if the agent removes it, the removal must be recorded and the piece rebuilt in the next round.
A fridge planned in the kitchen must be built as a standalone appliance, not as part of the kitchen_counter module; when the module build drops it, a library model must be assigned.
An exterior camera that must show a window must be positioned so the window is in frame; if the current pose misses it, the camera must be moved.
Drawn strokes on the furniture layer that form a group (sofa, chairs around a table) must be resolved into individual typed pieces by the reading stage, not left as unassigned strokes.
When a room outline holds two labels, the reading stage must split it into two rooms; a wall between them must be read or created.
A piece named in the documents (by a text label) must be built in the model; if the reading stage missed it, the agent stage must add it.
A piece removed by the agent must be rebuilt if the room's program still lists it; the removal reason must not hide a loss.
A cluster of drawn pieces larger than 4.5 m on a side must be broken into its constituent pieces by the reading stage, not left as a single untyped piece.
none
Site areas labeled as VERANDA or BALKON in the documents must be built as outlined platforms or terraces in the 3D model, even if they are not enclosed rooms.

A drawn piece that is 60% or more inside another piece's footprint is a detail of that piece and is not built as its own; an AI pass that names it a separate type (floor_lamp/nightstand) must not override that containment test, and the reading must not emit it as a standalone piece.
The reading stage must read ATTDEF (attribute definition) entities in a DWG, not skip them; they carry the text of block attributes (room labels, dimensions) that the ledger checks.
Site decor read on a level other than the ground floor (L0) is a duplicate of the ground plan's symbols and must be dropped by the site stage, not carried forward unused.
When a room outline holds two labels (e.g. a living room and a dining area), the reading stage must split it into two rooms at the wall between them, not merge them under one label.
A printed area label on a plan must be matched to its room and used for the area check; if the room's built area disagrees, the reading must flag it, not drop the label.
When walls are drawn as face lines on a chosen layer, the reading stage must also check the runner-up layer and any off-layer wall primitives that close a labelled room, not leave them out silently.

A layer whose name denotes a building element (e.g. DENIZLIK = bathtub) must be read and matched to the corresponding fixture; if none of its entities are used, the reading must flag it, not drop it silently.
An opening read twice (duplicate evidence) must be deduplicated by the build stage, not dropped; if it is gone after the build stage, the build must re-run to restore it.
The agent stage must not drop a drawn desk that the decor stage placed; if a desk is removed, the reason must be recorded and the piece restored or re-placed.

A labelled outdoor area (veranda, terrace, balcony) in the site plan must be built as a platform with its drawn outline, columns and glazing/railing; 'no outline' is a loss, not a valid reason to skip it.
A kitchen counter's top must be at working height (0.85-0.95 m); a counter read at 2.10 m is a misread size, not a tall cabinet.
A kitchen room's program requires a stove/hob; if the drawn stove is not built, the kitchen_run group must be completed with it.
A dining table in a furnished render must have styled surfaces (tablecloth, setting, or at least a centrepiece); a bare table is a missing layer.
A large blank wall behind a seating area in a living room must have wall art or a feature; an empty wall is a missing layer.
Sofas and armchairs in the same seating group must be from a compatible design family; a clash of styles is a mismatched_set.
A dining set (table + chairs) must be a unified group; a single mismatched chair is a mismatched_set.
A fridge in a kitchen must match the kitchen's material palette; a glossy black fridge in a matte warm kitchen is a mismatched_set.
A bedroom's listed pieces (desk, office chair, etc.) must be visible in the render; if they are missing after the agent stage, the agent must place them.
Two beds in the same room must be from a compatible design family; different headboards are a mismatched_set.
Armchairs in a bedroom must match the room's material palette; molded plastic in a warm neutral room is a mismatched_set.
A wardrobe listed in a bedroom's pieces must be visible in the render; if it is missing after the agent stage, the agent must place it.
A dresser listed in a bedroom's pieces must be visible in the render; if it is missing after the agent stage, the agent must place it.
A washbasin in a bathroom must be on a proper vanity, not a small shelf; a low-poly black box is a placeholder, not a styled fixture.

A labelled veranda, terrace, or balcony in the site plan must be built as a distinct platform with a floor, a parapet or railing, and a door or opening from the adjacent interior room. If the outline is missing, the site stage must reconstruct it from the plan lines before the building stage.

rules_proposed.rule: When a section prints the ground floor at a non-zero mark (e.g. +0.50), the reading must anchor the building's level 0 to the section's datum and shift every plan mark by that offset, so relative heights stay true; a systematic level offset must be corrected at the level frame, not per element.
A washbasin that is clashing with other furniture must be re-fitted by the agent. The fit stage must ensure that the washbasin is placed clear of other pieces and within the room's usable area.
Scene check S2 failures must be resolved by the agent. The fit stage must ensure that all scene checks pass before the render stage.

When a furniture name text names a piece type and no drawn piece of that type stands within 1 m of the text, add the piece at the text's position if the room allows the type and the spot is free, instead of dropping it because the nearest valid place is more than 1 m away.
The ground floor level mark in the section must be read as 0.00 m, not +0.50 m; all relative marks in the plans must be adjusted accordingly to avoid a systematic 0.50 m level error.

When a document names a storage piece (dresser, chest, sideboard) at a position that is more than 1 m from any valid placement in the room, and the room already contains a wardrobe or tall cabinet, the named piece is treated as a duplicate of the existing storage and is not built; the finding is closed as a false alarm. If the room has no other storage, the piece is placed at the nearest valid spot regardless of the 1 m tolerance, and the finding is closed as fixed.

A furniture piece must not sit on the clear opening of a window or door: the door/window ray check must reject any placement whose footprint intersects the opening's clear width, and the fitter must push the piece to the nearest free spot clear of the opening.

prevention.what: the model makes no sense to a visitor (a door into the air, a basin at knee height, stairs running into each other, a railing across a door)

rules_proposed.rule: A bathroom set (bathtub, washbasin, toilet) must be placed so no two members overlap; when the drawn bays are too tight, the solver must re-place the set as a unit rather than leave a clash for the architect.
A window or door opening must have a clear sight and passage line; furniture placed in front of an opening is a fit error and must be moved, not left to block the opening.
A kitchen counter's top must be at its working height (about 0.90-0.97 m); a counter built with its top at 2.10 m is a build error and must be rebuilt at the correct height.

An entrance with steps must have a handrail that is connected to the steps and a clear relationship between the door, the landing and the steps; a disconnected handrail or unclear step-door relationship is a build error.

A dressing room (or any 'other' room that is a suite component) must be directly connected to at least one bedroom or bathroom; a dressing room with no connection to a bedroom or bathroom is a layout error and must be flagged for the architect.

Every interior door must be built with a visible threshold (a 10-15 mm reveal or a flush threshold strip) and a frame that contrasts with the wall finish; the render stage must not present a door leaf flush with the floor and a frame indistinguishable from the wall as a finished joinery.

The entrance area must be clearly defined: the steps, the door, and any railing must form a coherent approach. The site stage must ensure that railings are connected to the steps or the building, and the overall flow to the entrance is legible in the render.

Balcony railings must be fully enclosed on all edges and use a material and style consistent with the building's finish; a simple metal tube railing is not acceptable for a stylish home. The site stage must ensure the railing model fully encloses the balcony edge and matches the building's material palette.

A room smaller than 4 m2 that is not connected to the entrance and contains only a shoe cabinet is a storage or utility space, not a hall. The layout stage must retype such rooms to 'storage' or 'other' and not label them as 'hall'.

A hall on an upper floor that is not connected to the entrance is a circulation space, not an entrance hall. The layout stage must label it as 'hall' (circulation) and not imply it is the main entrance. The entrance is on L0.

A bathroom that is not connected to any bedroom or hall is inaccessible and must be flagged. The layout stage must ensure that every bathroom is connected to at least one bedroom or the main circulation space. If a bathroom is isolated, it must be reconnected or retyped.

A bedroom that is not connected to any bathroom is acceptable if the building has a shared bathroom, but the layout stage must flag it for review. The finding is that the bedroom is not connected to a bathroom, which may be intentional (shared bathroom) or a layout error.
A dressing room must be directly connected to a bedroom or a bathroom; if it is not, it should be merged into an adjacent room or its type changed to 'storage' or 'hall'.

rules_proposed.rule: A kitchen room whose counter is built without its stove and wall cabinets is an incomplete kitchen run: the build stage must complete the run (counter + stove + wall cabinets) as one set, not ship a bare counter.
A room whose listed pieces (desk, office chair, armchairs, floor lamp) are absent from the build is a build loss: the furniture round must build every listed piece, not drop the secondary group.
A room whose only listed piece is absent from the build is a build loss: the furniture round must build every listed piece, even in a small hall.

An interior camera must frame the room's principal fixture (toilet in a bathroom, bed in a bedroom, counter in a kitchen); a view that shows the room but not its anchor piece is a failed view, not a missing piece.

A bed_double model that looks like a bed_single in a render (e.g. due to a low profile or a single-mattress appearance) must be swapped for a model that clearly reads as a double bed (two pillows, a wider frame) in the render.

rules_proposed.rule: Elevation checks that require a north arrow must be skipped if the north arrow is not present in the drawing. The reading stage must flag the absence of a north arrow and the check stage must not fail the elevation check for this reason.

A drawn section that does not run one-to-one with the plan (its ends are more than 0.30 m apart from the roof outline's ends along the cut direction) is not checked point by point against the roof; the roof is validated from its own roof_line entities instead.
An elevation that has neither a view bearing nor a side recorded is not compared with the model; the reading must assign each elevation a bearing or side before the check can run.
The big loop must run at least two full cycles before it may stop on a deadline, so that a first pass that only fixes geometry still gets a second pass to style and light the rooms.
A view that is marked for review must be re-evaluated in the next render cycle; a view left in review at the end of a run is a failed check, not a finished one.

When a drawn piece is left unbuilt because its cluster is larger than 4.5 m on a side, the reading stage must split the cluster into individual pieces (e.g. a wardrobe and a dresser) rather than discarding the whole cluster, so that each piece can be built and placed.

When an elevation sheet lacks a north arrow or side label, the pipeline must record the elevation's orientation from the plan's section cut line (its arrow direction) so that its openings can be checked against the plan; if no cut line is present, the check is skipped with an explicit 'orientation unknown' note rather than silently failing.

When a drawn section's ends do not align with the roof outline's ends (offset > 0.30 m), the pipeline must flag the section as 'not co-located with the plan' and skip the point-by-point roof check, recording the offset, rather than attempting a one-to-one comparison that will always fail.

Elevations without a view bearing or side label must be assigned an orientation from the plan's section cut lines or from their position relative to the building's north arrow before the render comparison stage; if no orientation can be derived, the comparison is skipped with an explicit note.
